conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’ve been admitted because of worsening swelling in your legs. Can you tell me how it’s been feeling lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been really bad. My legs are so heavy, and they’ve gotten bigger again, even after the last hospital stay. I can’t fit into my compression garments anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re about 20 pounds above your dry weight, which we estimate at around 360 pounds. We’ll work on reducing the fluid. We also want to make sure this isn’t an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not running a fever, but the skin is weeping a little. I was on penicillin for prevention, but my PCP thought I might have another cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on IV vancomycin just in case. But your white count isn’t very high, and you’re not febrile, so infection may not be the main issue. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on so many antibiotics. I’m worried about resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. Infectious disease reviewed your case and agreed the suspicion is low, but given your history, we’re treating it briefly just to be safe. We’ll stop it after five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray from last night shows no pneumonia or fluid in the lungs. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit short of breath. Is it my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your proBNP is only mildly elevated, and the X-ray doesn’t show heart failure. Your breathing issues might be from obesity and low lung volume. We’ll check your heart pressures with a right heart catheterization as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s scary because of my size. Will it be safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s low risk. It’s scheduled for day after tomorrow. It will help us see if your heart is contributing to the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg ultrasound came back. No blood clots were found in the major veins. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the calf veins weren’t seen. Could there still be a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The test was limited by your body habitus, but the main veins we can see are clear. We’re not concerned about DVT right now, especially since the swelling is equal on both sides.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is a bit worse today. Creatinine went from 1.1 to 1.7. This is likely from the diuretics and your baseline CKD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney failing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like a temporary change. It’s common with diuretics. We’ll monitor it and adjust your seizure meds if needed, since they’re cleared by the kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Keppra and Topamax. Will those be changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered the doses for now. If your kidney function improves, we’ll go back to your usual doses after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lymphedema team met with you today. They’re going to start compression wrapping to help with the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried that before. It helps, but it’s hard to keep up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re arranging for you to go to a rehab facility after discharge. They’ll help with daily wrapping and physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About a week or two, depending on progress. It’s to make sure you’re stable before going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just checking in after your right heart cath. It went well. Your heart pressures were borderline high, but your heart function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not heart failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not typical heart failure. The swelling is mostly from lymphedema and venous insufficiency, worsened by obesity. We’ll restart your bumetanide at 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 4 mg every other day. Is 2 mg daily stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a similar total dose but more consistent. We think that’s safer with your kidney function right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is improving—down to 1.3. That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I stop the IV fluids now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to oral diuretics. The IV Lasix was for rapid fluid removal. Now we’re maintaining with bumetanide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped the vancomycin today. Five days are complete. Penicillin prophylaxis is also stopped per infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t need any more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless you develop signs of infection—fever, redness, warmth. We didn’t see signs of active cellulitis, so we’re holding off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low yesterday—1.4. We restarted your warfarin at 6 mg. You’ll need a check in a few days after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a DVT before. Am I still at risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, so we’re keeping you on warfarin. Once your INR is therapeutic, we can stop the subcutaneous heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go directly to the rehab facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain? I’ve been using my oxycodone and Dilaudid as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve kept your pain regimen the same—45 mg oxycodone and 4 mg Dilaudid every six hours as needed. It’s stable and effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the nicotine patch. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve added the 21 mg patch daily to help with smoking. It’s part of your long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look good. White count is up a bit to 12.7, but no fever or other signs of infection. Likely from steroid effects or stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still wheezing a little. Is that my lungs or heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We heard some wheezing. It’s likely from your obesity and OSA. We’ve added albuterol nebs as needed. But you’re not on oxygen, and your saturation is 94% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. Rehab will continue your compression therapy and help with mobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home after rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. Watch for redness, fever, or increased pain in your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a vascular clinic follow-up scheduled in two weeks. Also, ID for a check-in, and your PCP for general care. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to leave. Your weight is down to 387 pounds. The swelling has improved, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a bit lighter, literally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with the compression, take your meds, and call if anything changes. You’ve done well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go to all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The rehab team knows your plan. They’ll help you transition home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It stays in. You may need IV meds or diuresis again. We’ll keep it maintained and flushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
